revisions.title: The method becomes the subject
revisions.body: I suggest hearing this stretch as a change in method. Parmenides asks us to take a subject as being and as not being, then trace what follows for the subject and for the others. The exercise is presented as thoroughgoing training meant to see the truth. For this transition, stay with the procedure being set out rather than supplying a verdict.

revisions.title: The one that is: a whole with parts
revisions.body: The second hypothesis begins with a distinction: “the one is” means that the One partakes of being, not simply that it is one. That makes the one-that-is a whole with two parts, “one” and “being.” Repeated division then makes its multitude unlimited, and the argument extends the result to number. Hear this as a deduction within the hypothesis, not as a claim about the One without qualification.

revisions.title: Predicates under pressure
revisions.body: After the whole is given limit, middle, and extremes, the argument pushes the One through paired relations: it is both in itself and in another, then both at rest and in motion. Sameness and difference make it like and unlike; contact is tested by adjacency and number. Hear the passage as a pressure test, not a final portrait.

revisions.title: A stricter second pass
revisions.body: The first pass lets the non-being One be altered: alteration yields coming-to-be and perishing, while no alteration yields neither, so the hypothesis produces both results. Parmenides then returns to the beginning and asks what “is not” means simply, defining it as complete absence of being before continuing. The restart narrows the terms for the next deduction.

revisions.title: When unity disappears, predicates collapse
revisions.body: Without the One, each Other is treated as a mass that appears one but breaks into indefinite multitude when examined. The argument then reverses course: because none is one, the Others are neither one nor many, and finally neither are nor appear as such. The closing sentence gathers the result as a universal pair of opposites, within the exercise’s hypotheses.
